recommendation.recommendation: Build a personalized opportunity feed filtered by major and interests, but do not launch it until listing freshness and quality are demonstrably solved — because the one respondent who cited a primary barrier named distrust of listing quality, not lack of features. The feed should open with a single, clear goal visible in the first 60 seconds (per the only open-ended response), and Columbia-specificity should be the explicit differentiator over Handshake and LinkedIn. AI-assisted application drafts are the secondary build, prioritized for active applicants once the core feed is trusted.
because: Across both rounds, every respondent who expressed a preference cited Columbia-specificity and personalized recommendations as the top reasons to use LionMatch over existing tools (n=2, Round 1, Q6).
Personalized recommendations received the highest average feature rating in Round 1 (exact figures unfetched but described as the clear leader across both respondents).

The sole Round 2 respondent named distrust of listing quality/freshness as the single biggest barrier to using LionMatch more (n=1, Round 2, Q3) — this is the only direct adoption-barrier signal in the dataset and it points to a prerequisite, not a feature.
AI-assisted application drafts was selected as the one feature the Round 2 respondent would actually use (n=1, Round 2, Q4), consistent with Round 1's feature ratings where it also ranked highly.
The only open-ended response (Round 2, Q5) emphasized simplicity, organization, and a single clear goal as the first-60-seconds requirement — suggesting UX clarity matters as much as feature depth.
Word of mouth was the only discovery channel reported in Round 1, indicating existing tools are not deeply embedded, which creates a genuine opening for LionMatch if it can establish trust quickly.
recommendation.confidence_reason: The entire dataset comprises 3 respondents across two rounds — every finding is a single data point or a two-person observation, making it impossible to distinguish signal from noise or generalize to the Columbia student population.
caveats: The listing-freshness barrier came from one active applicant; casual browsers or researchers may cite entirely different blockers (awareness, relevance, interface), which would shift the build priority.
AI-drafts preference may be inflated by the Round 2 respondent's active-applying status — students in earlier search stages may prioritize discovery features over application-assistance tools.

No demographic or major data was collected in either round, so it is unknown whether these preferences hold across STEM vs. humanities students, underclassmen vs. seniors, or any other meaningful segment.
The open-ended UX simplicity signal comes from a single quote and cannot be treated as a theme — it may be idiosyncratic to that respondent.
recommendation.next_question: What would make you trust that an opportunity listed on LionMatch is current and worth your time — and what would make you immediately doubt it? (open-ended, targeting 40+ respondents across class years and majors) — because the listing-trust barrier is the only adoption blocker surfaced so far, and understanding what 'trust signals' look like to students determines whether the fix is a data/ops problem (fresher scraping, verified postings) or a UX problem (timestamps, response-rate badges, peer confirmations), which are very different builds.
